newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax cuts to hit revenues more than expected.
newsitem.headline: German tax cuts to hit revenues more than expected.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel's planned tax reform will reduce government revenues by more than earlier forecast in the years 1999 through 2001, according to legislative proposals he unveiled on Friday.

The reform will reduce tax revenues for federal, state and local governments by 48.1 billion marks in 1999, the bills show, compared with a 44 billion mark estimate made in January when Waigel's tax commission first made its proposals.
When the reduction in the solidarity tax that will start next year is included, the 1999 tax shortfall rises to 55.9 billion marks. In 2000, the net shortfall is projected at 54.7 billion marks.
The shortfall is due to be partly made up by a rise in indirect taxes such as the value-added tax or petroleum tax. A one-point rise in VAT would bring in 15 billion marks.
Waigel told a news conference he is still aiming for a net reduction of about 30 billion marks in taxpayers' burden.
Cuts in income and corporate taxes will total 84 billion marks in 1999, and the reduction in the solidarity tax will lower taxpayers' burden by a further 7.5 billion marks.
But additions to revenue from the closing of tax breaks will total only 36.4 billion marks in 1999.
Social Democrat tax specialist Joachim Poss said the revenue shortfalls, which total 160 billion marks between 1999 and 2001, were not responsible policy.
